title: Advanced passive
theme: Impersonal passive (It is said that...), double passive (He is said to be...), causative have/get, passive with reporting verbs
goal: Student handles sophisticated passive structures used in journalism, academic prose, and formal speech.
connects_to: M06 (Cláusulas participiais) — extends passive thinking into participle clauses.
module_chunks: It is said / believed / thought / reported / claimed that...
She is thought to have done...
They are believed to have left...
We need this done by Friday

units.title: It is said that
units.grammar_focus: Impersonal passive with reporting verbs (It is said/believed/thought/reported/claimed that...)
units.real_life_context: You report common belief or unverified claim without naming a source — news writing, academic hedging.

grammar.sentence: _____ that exercise improves mental health.
grammar.explanation: Impersonal passive: "It + is/was + past participle (of reporting verb) + that-clause". The agent is omitted because the source is general or unspecified — common knowledge, expert opinion. Used heavily in news and academic prose.

grammar.sentence: _____ that the company will file for bankruptcy next week.
grammar.explanation: "It is reported that + clause" hedges the claim — the reporter isn't asserting the bankruptcy, just relaying what's being said. Useful for unverified or attributed claims.

grammar.sentence: _____ that the universe began with a Big Bang.
grammar.explanation: "It is thought that..." — present accepted theory or belief. Same pattern as "It is said/believed/considered/known".

grammar.sentence: Is said that he resigned yesterday.
grammar.answer: It is said that he resigned yesterday.
grammar.explanation: English requires "it" as dummy subject in impersonal passive — unlike Portuguese, where "se diz que" omits subject. "Is said that" is ungrammatical in English. Always "It is said that..."

grammar.passage: The investigation continues. It is reported that three witnesses came forward last night. It is believed that the suspect was acting alone. It cannot yet be confirmed that any property was stolen — but it is widely suspected that this is the work of the same group responsible for the previous incidents.
grammar.question: What is widely suspected?
grammar.answer: that this is the work of the same group responsible for previous incidents
grammar.explanation: Three impersonal passives layered ("It is reported... It is believed... It cannot be confirmed... it is widely suspected"). News register at its most cautious.

listening_speaking.text: It is said that money can't buy happiness.
It is believed that the painting is genuine.
It was once thought that the Earth was flat.
It is reported that talks have collapsed.
It cannot be denied that the project failed.

units.title: He is said to be
units.grammar_focus: Double passive — subject + is said/thought/believed + to + infinitive (or perfect/passive infinitive)
units.real_life_context: You report a claim about a specific person, fronting them as the subject instead of using "It is said that...".

grammar.sentence: He _____ to be the best surgeon in the country.
grammar.explanation: Double passive: subject + is said/believed/thought + to + infinitive. "He is said to be..." compresses "It is said that he is..." into one clause. More elegant and common in journalism.

grammar.sentence: She _____ to have left the country.
grammar.explanation: "She is believed to have left" = "It is believed that she has left". Perfect infinitive ("to have left") shows the leaving happened in the past, before the reporting.

grammar.sentence: They _____ to be considering a merger.
grammar.explanation: "They are thought to be considering" — continuous infinitive after "to". The subject "they" is reported as currently considering something.

grammar.sentence: He is said that he is wealthy.
grammar.hint: Either "It is said that he is wealthy" OR "He is said to be wealthy"
grammar.answer: He is said to be wealthy.
grammar.explanation: Don't mix the impersonal "It is said that" with the double passive "He is said to be". Two distinct structures — never combined. "He is said that he is" is ungrammatical hybrid.

grammar.passage: The CEO is said to be furious. She is reported to have demanded a complete review of last quarter's accounts. Two senior auditors are believed to have been dismissed since Monday. The company is thought to be preparing a public statement.
grammar.question: How many auditors are believed to have been dismissed?
grammar.explanation: Four double passives in succession ("is said to be... is reported to have demanded... are believed to have been dismissed... is thought to be preparing"). Journalism-grade compression.

listening_speaking.text: He is said to be a recluse.
She is believed to have left the country.
They are thought to be in talks.
The painting is reported to be a forgery.
He is rumoured to have made millions.

units.title: Have something done
units.grammar_focus: Causative have/get + object + past participle (services others perform for you)
units.real_life_context: You describe having someone else do something for you — haircut, repairs, dry-cleaning, surgery.

grammar.sentence: I _____ last week.
grammar.explanation: Causative pattern: "have + object + past participle". You didn't cut your own hair — you arranged for someone else to. "Had my hair cut" = arranged a haircut. Distinct from "I cut my hair" (did it yourself).

grammar.sentence: She _____ next week.
grammar.explanation: "Get + object + past participle" = informal causative. Same meaning as "having her car repaired". "Get" is more common in spoken English; "have" slightly more formal but both widely used.

grammar.sentence: We need to _____ this contract _____ by Friday.
grammar.explanation: "Have this contract reviewed by Friday" — passive causative with deadline. Implies the reviewing will be done by someone else (a lawyer, an editor), arranged by us.

grammar.sentence: "I cut my hair last week" (you mean someone else cut it).
grammar.hint: To make clear someone else did it, use causative
grammar.answer: I had my hair cut last week.
grammar.explanation: "I cut my hair" implies you did it yourself with scissors at home. To indicate a barber did it, use the causative: "I had/got my hair cut". Crucial precision in C1 communication.

grammar.passage: Before the conference, she had her speech proofread by a friend, got her suit pressed, and had her laptop checked for the third time. None of it stopped the nerves, but at least she could blame everything except her preparation.
grammar.question: What three things did she arrange to be done before the conference?
grammar.answer: speech proofread, suit pressed, laptop checked
grammar.explanation: Three stacked causatives — "had her speech proofread" (have), "got her suit pressed" (get), "had her laptop checked" (have). All passive causatives, all arranged by her but performed by others.

listening_speaking.text: I had my hair cut yesterday.

I need to have my eyes tested.
He had his portrait painted.

units.title: Get yourself done
units.grammar_focus: Get-passive nuance — unintended/negative events, and "have/get + something + done by + agent"
units.real_life_context: You distinguish causative ("I had it done") from passive misfortune ("I had my wallet stolen").

grammar.sentence: I _____ on the train yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "Have + object + past participle" can also describe MISFORTUNE — something done TO you against your will. "I had my wallet stolen" = my wallet was stolen (passive misfortune). Same surface structure as causative; context tells you which.

grammar.sentence: She _____ in the accident.
grammar.explanation: "Get + object + past participle" can also signal unintentional/unfortunate events. "Got her arm broken" — it happened to her, not by choice. "Broke her arm" is also fine but more neutral.

grammar.sentence: We _____ our house _____ while we were away.
grammar.explanation: "Had our house burgled" — passive misfortune, no agency on the homeowners' part. The structure mirrors causative but the meaning is its opposite.

grammar.sentence: I cut my hair by a hairdresser yesterday.
grammar.hint: To name the agent, use causative + "by"
grammar.answer: I had my hair cut by a hairdresser yesterday.
grammar.explanation: "I cut my hair" implies you did it. To attribute action to someone else AND name them, use causative + "by + agent". "I had/got my hair cut by..."

grammar.passage: Travelling alone, you learn quickly. By the end of the first week she had been pickpocketed once, had got her phone soaked in the rain, had had her booking cancelled by the hostel — and yet she remembered the trip as one of her best. Inconvenience, she discovered, is forgettable. Stories are not.
grammar.question: What three things happened to her in the first week?
grammar.answer: she was pickpocketed, got her phone soaked, had her booking cancelled
grammar.explanation: Three misfortunes in causative-form: "had been pickpocketed", "had got her phone soaked", "had had her booking cancelled". All passive events done to her, framed with "have/get + object + past participle".

listening_speaking.text: I had my wallet stolen on the train.
She got her car towed last night.
We had our flight cancelled twice.
He had his appeal rejected.
I had my coat ruined at the dry cleaner.

units.title: Mixed passive register
units.grammar_focus: Integration of impersonal passive, double passive, causative, get-passive across registers
units.real_life_context: You select the passive form that suits the register — formal news, conversational misfortune, arranged service.

grammar.sentence: _____ that climate change will affect food production within a decade.
grammar.explanation: Impersonal passive — formal hedged claim. "It is feared/predicted/anticipated that..." — academic and journalistic register.

grammar.sentence: She _____ to be one of the most influential thinkers of her generation.
grammar.explanation: Double passive: "She is considered to be..." compresses "It is considered that she is...". Common biographical register.

grammar.sentence: I need to _____ my passport _____ before I travel.
grammar.explanation: Causative: "Have my passport renewed" — arranging the service. Distinct from "renew my passport" (you doing the renewal yourself, which makes less sense since governments issue them).

grammar.sentence: I had stolen my bike last week.
grammar.hint: For misfortune, the structure is "had + object + past participle" (your bike was stolen)
grammar.answer: I had my bike stolen last week.
grammar.explanation: "I had stolen my bike" reads as "I had committed the theft of my bike" (past perfect active). To describe the misfortune of being stolen from, use "I had + object + past participle".

grammar.passage: Profiling the architect, the magazine wrote: 'She is widely regarded as one of the discipline's most original voices. It has long been said that her early studio drawings predicted half her later career. Even now, with three major commissions in progress, she still has her sketches reviewed by the same teacher who taught her at nineteen.'
grammar.question: Who reviews her sketches now?
grammar.answer: the same teacher who taught her at nineteen
grammar.explanation: Three passive registers stacked: "She is widely regarded" (double passive), "It has long been said" (impersonal passive perfect), "she still has her sketches reviewed" (causative). Profile writing at its layered best.

listening_speaking.text: It is feared that the crisis will deepen.
She is considered to be the leading expert.
I had my passport renewed last month.
I had my coat stolen at the gym.
He is rumoured to have signed a new contract.

cross_unit_consolidation: Form impersonal passive with reporting verbs (It is said/believed/thought/reported/claimed that...)
Compress to double passive (He is said to be... / She is thought to have done...)
Use causative "have/get + object + past participle" for arranged services
Use the same structure for passive misfortune (I had my wallet stolen)
Distinguish the two readings by context
Pair causative with "by + agent" when naming who did it
Recognise these registers in news, biography, and conversation
